segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He entered Jericho and was passing through it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, there was a man named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, since he was short in stature.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore fig tree to see him, because Jesus was about to pass that way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came to the place, Jesus looked up and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he hurried down and welcomed him joyfully.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all who saw it began to grumble, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has gone in to lodge with a sinful man.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, half of my possessions, Lord, I am giving to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I am paying it back fourfold.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were listening to these things, he went on to tell a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and they supposed that the kingdom of God was about to appear at once.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man of noble birth travelled to a distant country to receive kingship for himself and then return.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He called ten of his slaves, gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Do business with these until I come back.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And it happened that when he returned, having received the kingship, he ordered those slaves to whom he had given the money to be called to him, so that he might learn what they had gained by doing business.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The first came forward and said, ‘Master, your mina has earned ten minas more.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And he said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you proved faithful in a very small thing, have authority over ten cities.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The second came and said, ‘Your mina, Master, has made five minas.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And he said to this one too, ‘And you, be over five cities.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then the other came and said, ‘Master, look, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a cloth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man: you take up what you did not lay down and reap what you did not sow.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said to him, ‘Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked slave! You knew, did you, that I am a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Why then did you not put my money in the bank? And I, on my return, would have collected it with interest.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And to those standing by he said, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And they said to him, ‘Master, he has ten minas!’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them in front of me.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it happened that as he came near Bethphage and Bethany, at the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of the disciples,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into the village opposite, and as you enter it you will find a colt tied up, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you are to say this: ‘The Lord needs it.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had been sent went off and found it just as he had told them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why are you untying the colt?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Lord needs it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he went along, people were spreading their cloaks on the road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was now drawing near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the deeds of power they had seen,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Blessed is the one who comes, the king, in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I tell you, if these keep silent, the stones will cry out.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If only you had recognized on this day, even you, the things that lead to peace! But now they have been hidden from your eyes.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a palisade against you and surround you and hem you in on every side,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and they will dash you to the ground, you and your children within you, and they will not leave stone upon stone in you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written, ‘And my house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes were seeking to destroy him, and so were the leading men of the people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but they could not find what they might do, for all the people hung on his words as they listened.

notes.note: The tree is the sycamore fig, a large fig species common in the Jordan valley, with low spreading branches that are easy to climb. It is unrelated to the trees called sycamore in Europe and North America.

The Greek verbs for giving and paying back are in the present tense. Most interpreters take them as a resolution made on the spot in response to Jesus (“I hereby give”). A minority read them as Zacchaeus describing his existing practice, in defence against the crowd's charge that he is a sinner. The rendering leaves both readings open, though Jesus' words about salvation coming “today” favour the first.

The Greek word is the same one translated “kingdom” in verse 11, but here it means the royal title and power, since the man returns to rule his own country. First-century hearers knew the pattern. Local rulers travelled to Rome to be confirmed as king, and Josephus reports that when Herod's son Archelaus did so in 4 BC, a delegation from Judea followed to oppose him.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most older English versions soften it to “servants”, though several recent ones use “slaves”. Slaves in the ancient world were often entrusted with managing money and business for their owners.

A mina was a sum of money equal to one hundred drachmas, roughly three to four months' wages for a labourer. Each slave receives one mina. The amount is modest, which is why the king calls it “a very small thing” in verse 17.

It is not certain whether verse 26 is spoken by the king inside the story or by Jesus stepping outside it to address his hearers. The translation treats it as the king's words, because verse 27 continues without a break in the king's voice. Verse 25 is an interruption by the bystanders, and a few ancient witnesses omit it.

notes.traditional: The Lord has need of it
notes.note: The Greek word for “Lord” here is the same word translated “owners” in verse 33, so there is a play between the colt's owners and the Lord who claims it. The words could also be construed as “Its master needs it.” Most translations read it as the text does here.

The acclamation quotes Psalm 118:26, a psalm sung by pilgrims at the festivals, with “the king” added. The second line echoes the angels' song at Jesus' birth (Luke 2:14), but here the peace is located in heaven.

The Greek is a broken sentence, an “if” clause whose conclusion is never stated, as though the speaker were overcome. English versions either leave it unfinished or, as here, turn it into a wish. The verb is the same one translated “recognize” in verse 44.

In the Greek Old Testament, “visitation” is a set term for God coming to inspect his people, whether to rescue or to judge. The sense here is that God has come to Jerusalem in Jesus and the city has failed to recognize it. The siege language of verses 43–44 matches what the Roman army did to Jerusalem in AD 70.

Jesus combines Isaiah 56:7 with Jeremiah 7:11, where the prophet warned that the temple would not protect those who treated it as a hideout. The Greek word means a violent robber or bandit, not a sneak thief, and the “den” is literally a cave where such men take refuge.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the New Testament in parables and in Paul's self-descriptions, and translations divide between “servant”, “slave” and “bondservant”.
The same word covers “Lord”, “master”, “owner” and “sir”, and the choice in each context shapes how readers hear address to Jesus and wordplay such as verses 31–34.
In the plural, of Jesus' acts, it is rendered variously as “miracles”, “mighty works” and “deeds of power” across the Gospels and Acts, and should be uniform.
Used of the temple saying, the men crucified with Jesus, Barabbas and the Good Samaritan's attackers, and renderings vary between “thief”, “robber”, “bandit” and “rebel”.
Frequent across the Gospels and Acts, and “scribe” may suggest a mere copyist to modern readers, where alternatives such as “legal expert” or “teacher of the law” are also in use.
